notes:
I have gathered substantial material from Enduring Word (Guzik/Pentecostal-charismatic), Spurgeon's Treasury of David (Baptist), Gill's Exposition (older Baptist), Ellicott's Commentary (older Anglican), and the Desiring God search results (Reformed Baptist/Piper). I was unable to fetch full Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, or Methodist sources due to tool limits, and I'll note where I could not retrieve that material. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Psalm 103 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview / Authorship

**Traditional view:** Attributed to David, probably in his later years when he had a "keener sense of sin" and a deeper appreciation of pardon. Spurgeon calls this psalm "the Monte Rosa of the divine chain of mountains of praise."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**G. Campbell Morgan** calls it "perhaps the most perfect song of pure praise to be found in the Bible."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Ellicott** notes the psalm "has been compared to a stream which, as it flows, gradually acquires strength and volume till its waves of praise swell like those of the sea." He observes the psalmist "speaks throughout as much in the person of the community as his own." Nothing definitively dates the psalm.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

---

### v. 1: "Bless the LORD, O my soul; all that is within me, bless His holy name."

**Traditional reading:** "Bless" here does not mean man bestows something on God (impossible); it means to praise, thank, and honor God. David is addressing his own soul — preaching to himself. Spurgeon remarks, "Soul music is the very soul of music.… He soliloquizes, holds self-communion and exhorts himself, as though he felt that dulness would all too soon steal over his faculties."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**"All that is within me":** David wants whole-person worship — understanding, will, affections, and all inward faculties — not half-hearted or outward-only praise. James Montgomery Boice is quoted: "What a rebuke to much of what passes for praise in our assemblies. We come to church, but we leave our minds at home."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Gill** explains that "all that is within me" means all powers and faculties of the soul, including all graces wrought in him — faith, hope, love, joy. God, being a Spirit, must be worshipped "in spirit and in truth."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

**Spurgeon** adds: "Let others murmur, but do thou bless. Let others bless themselves and their idols, but do thou bless the LORD."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

---

### v. 2: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds."

**Repetition:** David repeats the call to his own soul, showing earnestness. Spurgeon says, "These first verses are a tuning of the harp, a screwing up of the loosened strings that not a note may fail in the sacred harmony."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**"Forget not all His benefits":** Memory is treacherous — "by a strange perversity, engendered by the fall, it treasures up the refuse of the past and permits priceless treasures to lie neglected." Praise should be rational, rooted in remembering what God has actually done. The Hebrew word (gemul) literally means "actions" or "dealings," but God's dealings are all benefits.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

**John Piper** preached on this verse: "David prods himself: Bless the Lord, soul; remember his benefits, speak of his wonders."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/forget-not-all-his-benefits

**Gill** notes God appointed the Lord's Supper under the Gospel as an ordinance specifically to help us remember His principal benefit — redemption by His Son — knowing our weak memories.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

---

### v. 3: "He who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases."

**Forgiveness first:** All traditional commentators agree David places forgiveness first intentionally — it is the chief benefit. Spurgeon: "Till iniquity is forgiven, healing, redemption, and satisfaction are unknown blessings." Maclaren is quoted: "The profound consciousness of sin, which it was one aim of the Law to evoke, underlies the psalmist's praise."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Augustine** (cited by Ellicott): "God's benefits will not be before our eyes unless our sins are also before our eyes" — implying a quickened moral sense.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

**"All" —** both "all iniquities" and "all diseases." The "all" gives confidence. Gill emphasizes it is a *continuing* act: "He 'forgiveth,' continues to forgive" — a continual flow of pardoning grace.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

**"Heals all your diseases":** A point of interpretive difference:

- **Literal/physical reading:** The Pulpit Commentary says this "is best understood literally — not as mere 'parallelism.'" Boice likewise insists David "really is speaking of diseases," arguing that "when we are healed, as we often are, it is God who has done it." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/ ; Pulpit Commentary cited via biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/103-3.htm

- **Spiritual reading:** Gill and Ellicott see "diseases" here as chiefly spiritual/moral (sin as a disease of the soul), based on the poetic parallelism with "iniquities." Gill: "Sin is a natural, hereditary, epidemical, nauseous, and mortal disease… healing diseases and forgiving iniquities are one and the same thing." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

- **Both/and:** Trapp allows both "corporal and spiritual" — "Jehovah Rophe… cureth his people on both sides, maketh them whole every whit." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/psalms-103.html

**Spurgeon** holds a both/and view: sickness came through sin, and "as sin is eradicated, diseases bodily, mental, and spiritual will vanish."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Pentecostal/charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik): says David "seems to refer to physical diseases" but also notes many commentators see them as spiritual. He leans toward the physical reading.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

### v. 4: "Who redeems your life from the Pit and crowns you with loving devotion and compassion."

**"The Pit" (shachat):** Ellicott renders it "pit, or grave, as in Psalm 16:10." The Targum reads "from hell." Gill explains this as redemption from eternal destruction — the second death. Christ "who is the Redeemer appointed and sent… has obtained eternal redemption; through which the saints are secure from going down to the pit of destruction."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

**"Redeems" (goel):** Adam Clarke sees a kinsman-redeemer image: "possibly looking forward, in the spirit of prophecy, to him who became partaker of our flesh and blood, that he might have the right to redeem our souls from death by dying in our stead."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**"Crowns you":** A metaphor from festive wreaths and garlands (Ellicott). Spurgeon: "Our Lord does nothing by halves… Cleansing, healing, redemption, are not enough, he must needs make them kings and crown them." The crown is "studded with gems of grace and lined with the velvet of lovingkindness."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

---

### v. 5: "Who satisfies you with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's."

**"Satisfies":** Spurgeon: "No man is ever filled to satisfaction but a believer, and only God himself can satisfy even him. Many a worldling is satiated, but not one is satisfied." The Hebrew can also be read as "filling with good thy soul" or (LXX/Vulgate) "thy desire."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

**"Youth renewed like the eagle's":** Traditional readings vary:

- **Spurgeon** rejects the moulting legend (though the KJV tradition alludes to it): "the original does not appear to allude to any such fact of natural history, but simply to describe the diseased one as so healed and strengthened, that he became as full of energy as the bird which is strongest of the feathered race."
- **Ellicott** says the psalmist "merely refers to the fresh and vigorous appearance of the bird with its new plumage," and notes the Rabbinical story and phoenix myth developed later.
- **Trapp** relays the ancient belief that the eagle renews its youth by casting old feathers and even beating its overgrown bill against a rock to recover eating — which Augustine allegorized: "That which hindereth our renovation… the rock Christ taketh away."
- **Kidner** (cited by Guzik): "The second line is not implying…that eagles have the power of self-renewal; only that God renews us to…the very picture of buoyant, tireless strength which Isaiah 40:30f. takes up."

— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/psalms-103.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Gill** reads it as spiritual renewal: "the youth of grace, or a renewal of spiritual love and affection to divine and heavenly persons and things… so that though the outward man may decay, yet the inward man is renewed day by day."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

---

### v. 6: "The LORD executes righteousness and justice for all the oppressed."

**Shift from personal to corporate:** David moves from personal mercies to God's dealings with His people and all the oppressed. Spurgeon: "Our own personal obligations must not absorb our song; we must also magnify the Lord for his goodness to others."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Trapp** notes the plural words in Hebrew "show that God will execute omnimodam iustitiam et iudicium, all and all manner of justice and judgment, relieving the oppressed, and punishing the oppressor to the full."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/psalms-103.html

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** ties this to God as "a father of the orphans and judge of widows."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-103.html

---

### v. 7: "He made known His ways to Moses, His deeds to the people of Israel."

**Reference to Exodus 33:13:** Ellicott affirms this is a direct reference to Moses' request "show me now Your ways." Gill details: God made known to Moses the order of creation, His ways of providence, His "way of grace and mercy, life and salvation, by Christ" — and the Law.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

**Two levels of revelation:** Moses received God's "ways" (the inner principles of His dealings), while Israel saw His "acts" (the outward deeds). Spurgeon: "They saw less than Moses, for they beheld the deeds of God without understanding his method therein."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Guzik** names this as "another aspect of God's greatness… His self-revelation. God could be content to hide Himself, but instead He wanted to make known His way and His acts."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

### v. 8: "The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion."

**Direct quotation of Exodus 34:6.** This was the great self-revelation of God to Moses, and Ellicott notes it "had become a formula of the national faith," also used in Joel 2:13, Psalm 145:8, and elsewhere.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**John Piper** (via Desiring God article) emphasizes that David "latches on to a particular text" — Exodus 34:6 — and "begins to spin out all its implications." Piper notes that Moses, Jonah, Jeremiah, Joel, Nehemiah, and Hezekiah all went to this same text for help.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/psalm-103-learning-how-to-talk-to-yourself

**Spurgeon** elaborates: "All the world tastes of his sparing mercy, those who hear the gospel partake of his inviting mercy, the saints live by his saving mercy, are preserved by his upholding mercy, are cheered by his consoling mercy, and will enter heaven through his infinite and everlasting mercy."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

---

### v. 9: "He will not always accuse us, nor harbor His anger forever."

**Spurgeon:** "He will sometimes, for he cannot endure that his people should harbour sin in their hearts, but not for ever will he chasten them; as soon as they turn to him and forsake their evil ways he will end the quarrel." God "bears no grudges."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Kidner** (cited by Guzik): "These very human terms point the contrast between God's generosity and the heavy-handed wrath of man, who loves to keep his quarrels going… and to nurse his grievances."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** notes: though God's anger "is reserved for the wicked" (citing Isaiah 57:16), with His own people He does not continue it forever.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-103.html

---

### v. 10: "He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities."

**Spurgeon:** "We ought to praise the Lord for what he has not done as well as for what he has wrought for us; even the negative side deserves our adoring gratitude." Else Israel — and we — would have perished.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Gill** explains: had God dealt with them according to the full demerit of sin, "they must have been sent to hell." The reason He does not is "because Christ has bore them, and the chastisement of them, and made satisfaction to divine justice for them."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

**Guzik** echoes: "David knew that his sins (and the sins of his people) deserved much greater judgment or discipline than they had received." A quote from Baker (in Spurgeon): "Why is it that God hath not dealt with us after our sins? Is it not because he hath dealt with another after our sins?"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

### v. 11: "For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him."

**Immeasurable mercy:** The distance between heaven and earth was the largest conceivable measurement. Spurgeon: "Boundless in extent towards his chosen is the mercy of the Lord; it is no more to be measured than the height of heaven."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Ellicott** notes the literal Hebrew is "Strong is his mercy upon (or over) them that fear him" and compares Genesis 49:26 — suggesting the sense "so far (above what was expected) for them fearing him prevails his mercy."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

**"Those who fear Him":** This qualification is crucial. Spurgeon warns: "Those who are presuming upon the infinite extent of divine mercy, should here be led to consider that although it is wide as the horizon and high as the stars, yet it is only meant for them that fear the Lord, and as for obstinate rebels, they shall have justice without mercy."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Piper** defines "fearing God" as meaning "God is so powerful and so holy and so awesome to us that we would not dare to run away from him, but only run to him for all that he promises to be for us." It is not a separate requirement from faith but "the way you come."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/bless-the-lord-o-my-soul

---

### v. 12: "As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us."

**Universally celebrated verse.** Spurgeon: "O glorious verse, no word even upon the inspired page can excel it!"

**The geometry of grace:** East and west, unlike north and south, have no meeting points on a globe — they are infinitely apart. Guzik: "If you travel north on a globe, you begin to travel south as soon as you go over the North Pole. But if you travel east, you will continue east forever."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Adam Clarke:** "As the east and the west can never meet in one point, but be for ever at the same distance from each other, so our sins and their decreed punishment are removed to an eternal distance by his mercy."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Gill** specifies this refers not to the removal of the *being* of sin but of guilt — ultimately through Christ's sacrifice: "Christ… by bearing them, removed the iniquity of the land in one day; and carried them away to the greatest distance… and upon the satisfaction he gave to divine justice, the Lord removed them both from him and them."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/103.htm

**Spurgeon:** "If sin be removed so far, then we may be sure that the scent, the trace, the very memory of it must be entirely gone.… there is no shade of fear of its ever being brought back again."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

---

### v. 13: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him."

**Paternal love:** Ellicott calls this "an anticipation of Christ's revelation of the paternal heart of God."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

**Maclaren** (cited by Guzik): "We may lose ourselves amid the amplitudes of the lofty, wide-stretching sky, but this emblem of paternal love goes straight to our hearts. A pitying God! What can be added to that?"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Spurgeon** elaborates the ways God pities: "our childish ignorance… our childish weakness… our childish foolishness… our childish naughtiness… our childish stumbles and falls… the pain of His children… the fears of His children." He emphasizes the present tense: "at this very moment he is now pitying them that fear him."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/ (citing Spurgeon)

**Piper** (Reformed Baptist): Preached an entire Father's Day sermon from this verse, stressing that good fathering points to God, and "perhaps nothing that you can do for your children to help them fear God… will be more effective than your own blessing the Lord continually in their presence."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/bless-the-lord-o-my-soul

---

### v. 14: "For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust."

**"Frame" (yetser):** Maclaren notes it literally means "formation" or "fashioning," from the same root as Genesis 2:7 ("the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground") and the potter's action in moulding clay (Isaiah 29:16).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Adam Clarke:** "In all his conduct towards us he considers the frailty of our nature, the untowardness of our circumstances, the strength and subtlety of temptation."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Incarnation connection:** Guzik notes that this pity "was turned to empathy at the incarnation. God Himself added humanity to His deity and experienced our frame and our dust-like weakness. What before He knew by observation, He submitted to know by experience."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

### vv. 15-16: "As for man, his days are like grass — he blooms like a flower of the field; when the wind passes over, it vanishes, and its place remembers it no more."

**Man's transience:** The "wind" here is the hot, scorching east wind (Ellicott). Matthew Poole notes "a flower of the field" is "more exposed to winds and other violences than the flowers of the garden, which are secured by the art and care of the gardener."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Ellicott** quotes Thomas Gray's Elegy to capture the pathos: "One morn I missed him on the accustomed hill… Another came, nor yet beside the rill, nor up the lawn, nor at the wood was he."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

---

### vv. 17-18: "But from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends to those who fear Him… to those who keep His covenant and remember to obey His precepts."

**The great contrast:** Man's moment vs. God's permanence. Meyer (cited by Guzik): "God's love does not alter with our alterings, or change with our changes. Does the mother's love fluctuate with the moods of her sick babe?" And: "There never was a time when He did not love you. His mercy is from everlasting; nor a time when He will love you less — it is to everlasting."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Conditional promises:** Guzik notes these promises "are made to those who fear Him, to those who keep His covenant, and those who remember His commandments to do them."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Piper** on the three conditions (fear Him, keep covenant, do commandments): "The requirement of obedience… is simply the requirement that our fear of God and our trust in Christ be real, effective, fruitful.… Our obedience, our righteousness, imperfect as it is, shows that God has saved us, that our faith is real."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/bless-the-lord-o-my-soul

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** references this as "His righteousness to children's children" — a generational blessing.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-103.html

---

### v. 19: "The LORD has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all."

**Divine sovereignty:** God's throne is "established" — fixed, immovable — in contrast to earthly thrones. His kingdom "rules over all" — no aspect of the universe is outside His reign.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Luther** (via Clarkson, in Spurgeon): When Melanchthon was extremely worried about church affairs, Luther admonished him: "Monendus est Philippus ut desinat esse rector mundi — Let not Philip make himself any longer governor of the world."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

### v. 20: "Bless the LORD, all His angels mighty in strength who carry out His word, who hearken to the voice of His command."

**Call to angels:** David expands the circle of praise from himself to the angels. Ellicott notes: "Just as in the highest revelation made by Jesus Christ the angels in heaven rejoice over the repentant sinner, so in the psalmist's view the mercy of Jehovah to his faithful people is cause for high acclaim among the hosts around the throne."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

**Guzik:** "David began the psalm by telling his own soul to bless the Lord, but he knew the praise and honor to God should go beyond what he could give. It should extend all the way to the angels."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

### v. 21: "Bless the LORD, all His hosts, you servants who do His will."

**Three grades of praise:** Ellicott discerns a hierarchy: (1) high angels around the throne (v. 20), (2) angelic powers — winds, lightnings, etc., specially commissioned (v. 21), and (3) all creation generally (v. 22).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/103.htm

**Guzik** sees the "hosts" as God's "heavenly army under His command who do His pleasure."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

### v. 22: "Bless the LORD, all His works in all places of His dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul!"

**Universal praise:** The psalm ends where it began — with David's own soul. Spurgeon: "Man is but little, yet, placing his hands upon the keys of the great organ of the universe, he wakes it to thunders of adoration! Redeemed man is the voice of nature, the priest in the temple of creation, the precentor in the worship of the universe."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**G. Campbell Morgan:** "The 'my' of personal experience merges into the 'our' of social fellowship, thus culminates in the 'all' of universal consciousness."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

**Kidner:** "His song is no solo, for all creation is singing — or will sing — with him; but his voice, like every other, has its own part to add."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

---

## Tradition-Specific and Other Views

### Where Protestant traditions differ

**Physical healing (v. 3):** This is the clearest point of difference.

- **Classic Reformed/Presbyterian, older Baptist (Gill), and Anglican (Ellicott)** read "heals all your diseases" primarily as spiritual healing — i.e., healing of the soul from sin. The parallelism with "forgives all your iniquities" supports this.

- **More recent evangelical/Pentecostal teachers (Guzik/Enduring Word, Boice)** insist the verse also means literal physical healing: "I think he really is speaking of diseases.… when we are healed, as we often are, it is God who has done it."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-103/

- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** holds a mediating view: sickness came through sin, and healing is both physical and spiritual, finding full fulfillment in the age to come.
  — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps103.php

**Covenant conditions (vv. 17-18):** Piper (Reformed Baptist) stresses that the promises are for "those who fear Him" and that fearing God is not a separate work but "the way you come" — humbly, reverently, without presumption. This is a classic Reformed emphasis on sovereign grace received through faith alone, not works.

**Note on Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran, Anglican, and Orthodox views:** I was unable to fetch dedicated sources from these traditions (e.g., seedbed.com, lcms.org, 1517.org, oca.org) due to search/fetch limits. The Ellicott commentary above represents an older Anglican perspective.

### Other views — where I could retrieve them

**Catholic and Orthodox:** Searches for newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org returned no results within available search calls. The Vulgate/LXX reading of v. 5 ("who filleth thy desire with good things") is noted by Ellicott and Gill — this is the Catholic Douay-Rheims textual tradition.

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible, bibleodyssey.org):** Unable to retrieve within search limits.

**Prosperity/Word of Faith/Hyper-grace:** No specific pages from these movements were found in the allowed search domains. Some might use Psalm 103:3-5 to support a guarantee of physical healing and material blessing in this life, but I could not locate a specific page documenting such a reading from within the allowed sites.
